renal-33.q: Leakage with coughing or sneezing in a multiparous woman is:
renal-33.e: Outlet incompetence from pelvic floor weakness; treat with pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, weight loss.

renal-33.q: Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity is treated with:
o: Midurethral sling to support the urethra
renal-33.e: Antimuscarinics (e.g., oxybutynin) or β₃ agonists (mirabegron) relax the detrusor. Overflow incontinence (incomplete emptying) uses catheterization; bethanechol helps an underactive detrusor; slings treat stress incontinence.

o: Weak pelvic floor with urethral hypermobility
renal-33.e: Bladder overfills and dribbles, e.g., BPH, diabetic neuropathy.

renal-33.q: A spinal cord transection above the sacral segments produces after spinal shock:
renal-33.e: Sacral reflex intact but no brain control (Guyton).

renal-33.q: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing diabetic neuropathy reports frequent small-volume urine leakage day and night without urgency. Her bladder is palpable after voiding, and the post-void residual volume is 450 mL. What is the underlying mechanism of her incontinence?
o: Urethral hypermobility from pelvic floor weakness
Inability to reach the toilet from poor mobility
renal-33.e: A large post-void residual with dribbling is overflow incontinence from an atonic (neuropathic) bladder. Involuntary detrusor contractions cause urge incontinence, with sudden urgency and a normal residual.

renal-47.q: Which diuretic class acts on the thick ascending limb?
renal-47.e: PCT: acetazolamide; TAL: loops (NKCC2); DCT: thiazides (NCC); collecting duct: K⁺-sparing.

o: Distal convoluted tubule and connecting tubule
Proximal tubule and thin descending limb
renal-47.e: It is filtered but not reabsorbed, so it holds water in the tubule by osmotic effect.

renal-47.q: Which diuretic acts on the collecting duct?
Loop diuretics produce the greatest natriuresis because the TAL:
o: Reabsorbs most filtered glucose via SGLT2
Is where ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels
renal-47.e: Up to 20–30% of filtered Na⁺ can be excreted.

renal-47.q: A 56-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis has tense ascites and a low urine Na⁺/K⁺ ratio. He is started on the diuretic of first choice for this condition, which counteracts his secondary hyperaldosteronism. At which nephron site does this drug act?
renal-47.e: Spironolactone is first-line for cirrhotic ascites and blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor in principal cells of the cortical collecting duct. Loop diuretics (thick ascending limb) are added second.

renal-48.e: It first expands ECF volume, which can precipitate pulmonary edema; also contraindicated in anuria.

o: Treat hyperkalemia by shifting K⁺ into cells
Treat edema in congestive heart failure
renal-48.e: Osmotic agent draws water out of tissues.

o: Blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
renal-48.e: Filtered, not reabsorbed: it raises tubular fluid osmolarity and so limits water reabsorption.

renal-48.q: A serious adverse effect of mannitol is:
renal-48.e: Contraindicated in anuria and heart failure.

renal-48.q: A 67-year-old man with a history of heart failure has a traumatic brain injury with signs of raised intracranial pressure and receives a large IV dose of mannitol. Two hours later he is dyspneic, with bibasilar crackles and an elevated JVP. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Water shift from cells into the ECF
renal-48.e: Mannitol stays in the ECF and pulls water out of cells, transiently expanding ECF volume and precipitating pulmonary edema in heart failure. It does not depress the myocardium directly.

renal-49.q: Acetazolamide is used for all EXCEPT:
renal-49.e: Also used for metabolic alkalosis; side effects include paresthesias, NH₃ toxicity and sulfa allergy.

renal-49.q: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase mainly in the:

renal-49.e: Metabolic acidosis stimulates ventilation; also glaucoma.

renal-49.q: A 32-year-old woman starts a drug the day before trekking to 5000 m to prevent altitude sickness. On day 1 her urine pH is 7.5. By day 3 she notes tingling in her fingers, and her serum HCO₃⁻ is 18 mEq/L with a normal anion gap. The drug's main effect results from inhibition of which process?
renal-49.e: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the PCT, causing early bicarbonaturia (alkaline urine) and then a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation at altitude; the bicarbonaturia is self-limited as serum HCO₃⁻ falls. Thiazides act on the distal Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter and cause alkalosis.

o: Epithelial Na⁺ channel (ENaC) in principal cells
renal-50.e: Abolishes the medullary gradient; also stimulates PGE release (blunted by NSAIDs).

renal-50.q: Which effect of loop diuretics is used to treat hypercalcemia?
renal-50.e: Loops lose calcium (Loops Lose Ca²⁺); thiazides do the opposite. Toxicities: Ototoxicity, Hypokalemia, Hypomagnesemia, Dehydration, Allergy (sulfa), Alkalosis, Nephritis, Gout (OHH DAANG).

renal-50.q: A patient with a sulfa allergy needs a loop diuretic. Best choice:
renal-50.e: Ethacrynic acid is not a sulfonamide but is more ototoxic and can cause hyperuricemia.

renal-50.q: A 66-year-old woman with acute decompensated heart failure receives repeated high-dose IV boluses of a diuretic that is also used to treat hypercalcemia. She then reports tinnitus and reduced hearing. Which transporter does this drug inhibit?
renal-50.e: Furosemide blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, increasing Ca²⁺ excretion; it is ototoxic, especially with rapid high doses. NCC is the thiazide target, and thiazides reduce urinary Ca²⁺.

renal-51.q: Thiazides are useful in calcium stones because they:
renal-51.e: Increased Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the DCT; also used in osteoporosis and nephrogenic DI.

renal-51.q: Which is an adverse effect of thiazides?
renal-51.e: HyperGLUC: hyperGlycemia, hyperLipidemia, hyperUricemia, hyperCalcemia; also hypokalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic alkalosis.

renal-51.q: Paradoxical use of a thiazide treats which disorder?
renal-51.e: Mild volume depletion ↑ proximal Na⁺/water reabsorption → less water reaches the collecting duct.

renal-51.q: A 52-year-old man starts a first-line antihypertensive. Six weeks later he has a hot, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Labs: uric acid 9.8 mg/dL, Ca²⁺ 10.8 mg/dL, glucose 128 mg/dL, K⁺ 3.3 mEq/L. Which drug was most likely started?
renal-51.e: Thiazides cause hyperuricemia (gout), hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia and hypokalemia. Losartan is mildly uricosuric and tends to raise rather than lower K⁺.

renal-52.q: Which K⁺-sparing diuretic directly blocks ENaC?
renal-52.e: Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone and eplerenone are aldosterone receptor antagonists.

renal-52.q: Gynecomastia in a man on a diuretic suggests:
renal-52.e: Spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors. Eplerenone is more selective. All K⁺-sparing agents risk hyperkalemia.

renal-52.q: Drug of choice for lithium-induced nephrogenic DI:
renal-52.e: Amiloride blocks lithium entry into principal cells via ENaC.

renal-52.q: A 61-year-old man with heart failure (EF 30%) takes lisinopril and furosemide. A drug is added to reduce mortality. Four weeks later he has tender breast enlargement and a serum K⁺ of 5.6 mEq/L. What is the mechanism of the added drug?
o: Direct blockade of ENaC in principal cells
Inhibition of Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransport in the DCT
renal-52.e: Spironolactone improves survival in HFrEF; it blocks the aldosterone receptor and, through antiandrogen effects, causes gynecomastia. Amiloride blocks ENaC directly and does not cause gynecomastia.

renal-53.e: Volume contraction (↑ AT II → NHE3) and K⁺ loss (H⁺ shifts into cells, ↑ H⁺ secretion). Acetazolamide and K⁺-sparing agents cause acidosis.

renal-53.q: Which diuretic class increases urinary NaCl and causes HYPOkalemia?
renal-53.e: Loops and thiazides deliver more Na⁺ to the collecting duct → ↑ K⁺ secretion.

renal-53.q: Thiazides cause which calcium and uric acid changes?
renal-53.e: Increased distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; reduced urate secretion.

renal-53.q: Loop diuretics cause which magnesium/calcium change?
renal-53.e: Abolishing the lumen-positive voltage reduces paracellular Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

renal-53.q: A 63-year-old woman takes a diuretic for edema. Labs: Na⁺ 137 mEq/L, K⁺ 3.1 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 31 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ 1.3 mg/dL, and 24-hour urine calcium is increased. Which diuretic is she most likely taking?
renal-53.e: Loop diuretics cause hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia and hypercalciuria. Thiazides cause the same alkalosis but decrease urinary calcium.

renal-54.e: GFR depends on efferent constriction by AT II; blocking it can cause AKI. Also contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal renal damage) and hereditary angioedema.

renal-54.q: Persistent dry cough on lisinopril is due to:
renal-54.e: Switch to an ARB, which does not raise bradykinin.

renal-54.q: Effect of ACE inhibitors on renin and angiotensin II:
renal-54.e: Loss of negative feedback raises renin; ACE blockade lowers AT II. Also ↓ GFR, ↑ K⁺.

renal-54.q: A 64-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension has bruits over both flanks. One week after he starts lisinopril, his creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.4 mg/dL. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Loss of angiotensin II efferent constriction
Direct toxic injury to tubular cells
renal-54.e: With bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole; ACE inhibition removes it and GFR falls. Loss of prostaglandin afferent dilation is the NSAID mechanism.

renal-55.e: ARBs (-sartans) share ACE-I effects (hyperkalemia, ↓ GFR, teratogenic) but do not raise bradykinin.

renal-55.q: Compared with ACE inhibitors, ARBs are less likely to cause:
o: Acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis
renal-55.e: Angioedema can still occur but is rarer.

renal-55.q: ARBs differ from ACE inhibitors because they do not increase:
A 33-year-old woman whose hypertension is well controlled on losartan has a positive pregnancy test at 7 weeks. She is switched to labetalol. The main fetal risk of continuing her original drug is:
renal-55.e: ARBs and ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic: they impair fetal renal development, causing oligohydramnios and its sequelae. Ebstein anomaly is linked to lithium, and neural tube defects to valproate.

renal-56.e: Blocks conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ↓ AT II and aldosterone.

renal-56.q: Aliskiren should be avoided with ACE inhibitors or ARBs in patients with:
renal-56.e: Combining RAAS blockers raises risk of hyperkalemia, hypotension and AKI.
Direct renin inhibitor blocks angiotensinogen → Ang I.

renal-56.q: A notable adverse effect of aliskiren is:
A 58-year-old man with hypertension is started on aliskiren. Compared with baseline, which laboratory pattern is expected after several weeks?
renal-56.e: Aliskiren blocks renin's catalytic site, so plasma renin activity and angiotensin II both fall even though renin concentration rises. ACE inhibitors raise PRA while lowering angiotensin II.

kub-embryology:s1.q: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the collecting ducts, calyces, renal pelvis and ureter?
kub-embryology:s1.e: The ureteric bud (outgrowth of the mesonephric duct) forms the collecting system: collecting ducts → calyces → pelvis → ureter.

kub-embryology:s1.q: Metanephric mesenchyme normally forms which part of the nephron?
kub-embryology:s1.e: Reciprocal induction with the ureteric bud makes the metanephric mesenchyme form glomerulus → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT.

kub-embryology:s1.q: Which part of the ureter is the last to canalize and the most common site of congenital obstruction?
kub-embryology:s1.e: The UPJ canalizes last; incomplete canalization is the most common pathologic cause of prenatal hydronephrosis.

kub-embryology:s1.q: A 16-year-old girl has primary amenorrhea with normal breast development and pubic hair. Pelvic imaging shows an absent uterus and upper vagina, normal ovaries, and absence of the right kidney. Her genital-duct and renal anomalies share origin from which embryonic region?
kub-embryology:s1.e: The kidneys, gonads and genital ducts all derive from intermediate mesoderm, so Müllerian agenesis (MRKH) often coexists with renal anomalies. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites (vertebrae, skeletal muscle).

kub-embryology:s2.q: The pronephros appears in week 4 and:
o: Persists to form the adult kidney
kub-embryology:s2.e: Rudimentary, cervical, regresses by end of week 4.

kub-embryology:s2.q: The nephric (mesonephric/Wolffian) duct grows caudally to open into the:
kub-embryology:s2.e: It later gives off the ureteric bud near its cloacal end.

kub-embryology:s2.q: A 29-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. Examination shows an absent left vas deferens; ultrasound shows an absent left kidney. Sweat chloride and CFTR testing are normal. Both anomalies most likely reflect abnormal development of which structure?
kub-embryology:s2.e: The mesonephric duct forms the vas deferens and also gives rise to the ureteric bud, so an early defect causes ipsilateral absence of the vas deferens and renal agenesis. The paramesonephric duct regresses in males.

kub-embryology:s3.q: A stillborn infant has pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened nose, low-set ears and clubbed feet. What is the trigger of this sequence?
kub-embryology:s3.e: Potter sequence: oligohydramnios compresses the fetus → limb and facial deformities and pulmonary hypoplasia (cause of death).

kub-embryology:s3.q: Which of the following can cause Potter sequence?
o: Unilateral renal agenesis with a normal contralateral kidney
kub-embryology:s3.e: Anything that cuts fetal urine output (bilateral agenesis, ARPKD, posterior urethral valves) or amniotic fluid (PPROM, placental insufficiency) causes it.

kub-embryology:s3.q: The primary cause of the flattened face and limb deformities in Potter sequence is:
kub-embryology:s3.e: Lack of fetal urine → oligohydramnios → compression and pulmonary hypoplasia.

kub-embryology:s3.q: The usual cause of death in Potter sequence is:
kub-embryology:s3.e: Amniotic fluid is needed for lung development.

kub-embryology:s3.q: Unilateral renal agenesis results from failure of which structure to develop?
kub-embryology:s3.e: Without the ureteric bud the metanephric mesenchyme is never induced, so that kidney does not form. Often found incidentally.

kub-embryology:s3.q: A patient with unilateral renal agenesis usually shows which finding in the remaining kidney?
kub-embryology:s3.e: The solitary kidney hypertrophies; these patients have a higher risk of hyperfiltration injury later.

kub-embryology:s3.q: The ureteric bud normally induces which tissue to form nephrons?
kub-embryology:s3.e: Reciprocal induction between ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme.

kub-embryology:s3.q: A 20-week prenatal ultrasound shows anhydramnios, no visible kidneys in either renal fossa, and a bladder that never fills. Which developmental event most likely failed?
o: Septation of the cloaca by the urorectal septum
Fusion of the metanephric blastemas at the lower poles
Outgrowth of the ureteric bud from the mesonephric duct
Canalization of the ureter at the pelvic junction
kub-embryology:s3.e: Bilateral renal agenesis results from failure of the ureteric buds to form, so the metanephric blastema is never induced and no fetal urine is made (Potter sequence). UPJ canalization failure causes hydronephrosis, not absent kidneys.

kub-embryology:s4.q: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is caused by:
o: Obstruction at the ureterovesical junction in adults
kub-embryology:s4.e: MCDK is a nonfunctional kidney of cysts and connective tissue from failed induction; it is usually unilateral and non-inherited.

kub-embryology:s4.q: A newborn has a unilateral flank mass of noncommunicating cysts with no function on imaging. Prognosis is good when:
kub-embryology:s4.e: Unilateral MCDK with a normal other kidney carries an excellent prognosis; bilateral disease leads to Potter sequence.

kub-embryology:s4.q: Unlike ARPKD, multicystic dysplastic kidney is usually:
kub-embryology:s4.e: MCDK is usually unilateral, sporadic, with a normal opposite kidney.

kub-embryology:s4.q: MCDK results from abnormal interaction between:
o: Pronephros and the caudal mesonephric duct
kub-embryology:s4.e: Failed induction yields noncommunicating cysts and dysplastic stroma.

kub-embryology:s4.q: A duplex collecting system arises from:
o: Ureteric bud splitting before it meets the blastema
Persistent urachus from incomplete allantois closure
Failure of the urorectal septum to divide the cloaca
Fusion of the lower kidney poles
kub-embryology:s4.e: The ureteric bud bifurcates before it enters the metanephric blastema. Bifid ureter or two ureters drain one kidney. It is strongly associated with vesicoureteral reflux and ureterocele.

kub-embryology:s4.q: In a complete duplex system, which ureter (Weigert–Meyer rule) typically obstructs?
o: Both ureters, at a common orifice
kub-embryology:s4.e: Upper pole: inserts ectopically, low and medial, and tends to obstruct (ureterocele). Lower pole: inserts higher and laterally and tends to reflux.

kub-embryology:s4.q: A bifid (partially duplicated) ureter results from:
o: Failure of ascent from the pelvis
Two separate ureteric buds from one duct
Early splitting of a single ureteric bud
kub-embryology:s4.e: Early division of one bud gives a Y-shaped ureter; two buds give complete duplication.

kub-embryology:s4.q: In a complete duplex system, the upper-pole ureter typically:
o: Drains the lower pole of the kidney
Inserts superolaterally and tends to reflux
Inserts inferomedially and tends to obstruct
Is congenitally absent on that side
kub-embryology:s4.e: Weigert–Meyer rule: the upper-pole ureter inserts ectopically and inferomedially and obstructs (ureterocele); the lower pole refluxes.

kub-embryology:s4.q: A 5-year-old girl voids normally but is constantly damp with urine throughout the day. Imaging shows a complete duplex collecting system on the left. Which finding best explains her symptoms?
o: Upper-pole ureter opening below the sphincter
Lower-pole ureter opening below the sphincter
Upper-pole ureter refluxing at the trigone
Lower-pole ureter refluxing at the trigone
kub-embryology:s4.e: By the Weigert–Meyer rule, the upper-pole ureter inserts inferomedially and may be ectopic distal to the external sphincter in girls, causing continuous dribbling with normal voids. The lower-pole ureter typically refluxes.

kub-embryology:s5.q: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into:
o: Bladder and the definitive pelvic urethra
kub-embryology:s5.e: Anterior urogenital sinus, posterior anorectal canal.

kub-embryology:s5.q: The trigone of the bladder is initially derived from:
o: Surface ectoderm of the cloacal membrane

kub-embryology:s5.e: Urachal fistula (urine leaking from the umbilicus), cyst or sinus.

kub-embryology:s5.q: A 54-year-old man has painless hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a mass at the bladder dome, and biopsy shows mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma. This tumor most likely arose from a remnant of which embryonic structure?
kub-embryology:s5.e: Urachal remnants lie at the bladder dome and can give rise to adenocarcinoma. The urogenital sinus forms most of the bladder, which normally gives rise to urothelial carcinoma.

kub-embryology:s6.q: During ascent, a horseshoe kidney gets trapped beneath which structure?
kub-embryology:s6.e: The fused inferior poles hook under the IMA, so the kidney stays low in the abdomen.

kub-embryology:s6.q: Horseshoe kidney is classically associated with which chromosomal disorder?
kub-embryology:s6.e: Associated with Turner syndrome and trisomies 13, 18 and 21; raises risk of hydronephrosis, stones, infection and some tumors.

kub-embryology:s6.q: Horseshoe kidney most often fuses at the:
kub-embryology:s6.e: Lower poles fuse; ascent stops at the inferior mesenteric artery.

kub-embryology:s6.q: A complication more common with horseshoe kidney is:
kub-embryology:s6.e: Abnormal ureter course predisposes to obstruction, infection and stones; also Wilms tumor risk.

kub-embryology:s6.q: A 14-year-old girl with short stature, a webbed neck and primary amenorrhea has abdominal ultrasound showing kidneys fused across the midline at their lower poles, lying lower than normal. The kidneys failed to ascend because they were trapped by which structure?
kub-embryology:s6.e: A horseshoe kidney (associated with Turner syndrome) ascends until the fused isthmus catches beneath the inferior mesenteric artery. The SMA arises higher and is the structure compressing the left renal vein in nutcracker syndrome.

kub-embryology:s7.q: Fetal urine begins to be produced at about:
kub-embryology:s7.e: Glomeruli start functioning around week 10–12; urine contributes to amniotic fluid.

kub-embryology:s7.q: Nephron formation (nephrogenesis) is complete by about:
kub-embryology:s7.e: No new nephrons form after ~34–36 weeks; kidneys grow by enlarging.

kub-embryology:s7.q: A man born at 26 weeks' gestation develops hypertension and early chronic kidney disease in his twenties, earlier than his term-born siblings. Which developmental factor most likely contributed?
kub-embryology:s7.e: Nephrogenesis continues until about weeks 34–36, so very preterm birth leaves fewer nephrons, predisposing to hyperfiltration, hypertension and CKD. Fetal urine production begins around week 10–12, well before this birth.

kub-embryology:s8.q: Posterior urethral valves occur only in:
kub-embryology:s8.e: A membrane remnant in the posterior (prostatic) urethra obstructs outflow in boys, the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants.

kub-embryology:s8.q: Prenatal ultrasound of a male fetus shows a thick-walled bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis and oligohydramnios. Most likely cause:
kub-embryology:s8.e: Outlet obstruction → bladder hypertrophy, bilateral hydronephrosis and low fetal urine (risk of Potter sequence).

kub-embryology:s8.q: Posterior urethral valves are best diagnosed after birth by:
kub-embryology:s8.e: VCUG shows a dilated posterior urethra and valve leaflets.

kub-embryology:s8.q: Posterior urethral valves arise in the:
kub-embryology:s8.e: Membranous folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra obstruct outflow.

kub-embryology:s8.q: A newborn boy has a distended bladder, a weak urinary stream and bilateral hydronephrosis. Voiding cystourethrography shows a dilated posterior urethra with an abrupt narrowing. Pregnancy was complicated by severe oligohydramnios. In severe cases, the main cause of neonatal death is:
kub-embryology:s8.e: Posterior urethral valves reduce fetal urine output and cause oligohydramnios, which impairs lung development; pulmonary hypoplasia is the main cause of early death. Infection and renal failure are later problems.

o: Inner lip of the iliac crest
kub-anatomy:wall.e: It shares this insertion with iliacus (iliopsoas).
Psoas major is supplied by anterior rami of L1–L3.
Inferiorly to the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament.

kub-anatomy:wall.q: The psoas major is innervated by:
kub-anatomy:wall.e: Direct branches from lumbar anterior rami.

kub-anatomy:wall.q: A 34-year-old man who injects drugs has fever and lower back pain and walks with his right hip held flexed. CT shows a fluid collection within the right psoas major. Which maneuver most likely worsens his pain?
o: Passive internal rotation of the flexed hip
kub-anatomy:wall.e: A psoas abscess makes stretching the inflamed muscle painful, so passive hip extension provokes pain (psoas sign). Pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign.

kub-anatomy:loc.q: Between which vertebral levels do the kidneys normally lie?
kub-anatomy:loc.e: Retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall, T12–L3; the right kidney sits slightly lower.

kub-anatomy:loc.q: Why does the right kidney usually lie lower than the left?
o: The spleen pushes the left kidney up
The right renal artery is shorter
kub-anatomy:loc.e: The large right lobe of the liver displaces the right kidney inferiorly.

o: Stay fixed by the renal fascia

kub-anatomy:loc.q: The hilum of the left kidney lies at about the level of:

A 47-year-old woman has a percutaneous nephrolithotomy through an upper-pole access above the 12th rib. Afterwards she is short of breath, with absent breath sounds at the right base. Which structure was most likely injured?
kub-anatomy:loc.e: The upper pole lies at T12, behind the diaphragm and the costodiaphragmatic recess of pleura, so supracostal access risks pneumothorax or hydrothorax. The colon and duodenum lie anterior to the kidney, not on a posterior track.

kub-anatomy:rel.q: Which structure contacts the anterior surface of the right kidney directly, without peritoneum between them?
kub-anatomy:rel.e: The descending (2nd) part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal; the liver and small intestine are separated from the kidney by peritoneum.

kub-anatomy:rel.q: Moving medial to lateral, which muscle is the most lateral posterior relation of the kidney?
kub-anatomy:rel.e: Posteriorly: diaphragm above, then psoas major → quadratus lumborum → transversus abdominis.

kub-anatomy:rel.q: Which nerve passes posterior to the kidney on quadratus lumborum?
The left kidney is related anteriorly to all EXCEPT:
kub-anatomy:rel.e: The second part of the duodenum lies anterior to the right kidney.

kub-anatomy:rel.q: After an open right nephrectomy through a flank incision, a 59-year-old man has numbness over the suprapubic skin and the upper lateral buttock. Which nerve, lying posterior to the kidney on quadratus lumborum, was most likely injured?
kub-anatomy:rel.e: The iliohypogastric nerve (L1) runs behind the kidney on quadratus lumborum and supplies the suprapubic skin and the lateral gluteal region. The genitofemoral nerve lies on the anterior surface of psoas and supplies the scrotum/labia and the upper anterior thigh.

kub-anatomy:fascia.q: What is the correct order of the coverings from the kidney outward?
o: Renal fascia → renal capsule → perirenal fat → pararenal fat
Perirenal fat → renal capsule → pararenal fat → renal fascia
Renal capsule → perirenal fat → renal fascia → pararenal fat
Renal capsule → pararenal fat → renal fascia → perirenal fat
kub-anatomy:fascia.e: Pararenal (paranephric) fat lies outside the renal (Gerota) fascia, mostly posterior and posterolateral.

kub-anatomy:fascia.q: Relative to the renal fascia, the suprarenal gland is:
o: Outside it, in the pararenal fat
Inside it, in a separate compartment
kub-anatomy:fascia.e: It lies inside the renal fascia but is separated from the kidney by a thin septum, so a ptotic kidney can drop without taking the suprarenal gland with it.
Pararenal fat lies outside the renal fascia, between it and the peritoneum/posterior abdominal wall. Perirenal fat is inside the renal fascia.

o: Nowhere; it is a closed sac
kub-anatomy:fascia.e: Infection or fluid may track inferiorly into the pelvis.

kub-anatomy:fascia.q: A 62-year-old man with diabetes has a perinephric abscess. CT shows the collection tracking downward along the psoas toward the pelvis, but it has not crossed to the opposite side. Why can the infection spread inferiorly?
o: Renal fascia layers are unfused inferiorly
Renal fascia is open across the midline
Perirenal fat opens into the peritoneum
Renal capsule is absent at the lower pole
kub-anatomy:fascia.e: The anterior and posterior layers of renal fascia are fused above and laterally but open inferiorly around the ureter, so perirenal fluid can track down into the pelvis. Medially, the fascia attaches around the great vessels and limits spread across the midline.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: From anterior to posterior, what is the order of structures at the renal hilum?
o: Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis
Renal pelvis, renal artery, renal vein
Renal vein, renal pelvis, renal artery
Renal artery, renal vein, renal pelvis
kub-anatomy:struct.e: VAP: vein anterior, artery in the middle, pelvis posterior.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: Minor calyces receive urine directly from the:
o: Cortical collecting ducts in medullary rays
Major calyces of the renal pelvis
Papillary ducts opening on a renal papilla
kub-anatomy:struct.e: Several minor calyces unite into a major calyx; 2–3 major calyces form the renal pelvis.

o: Renal sinus fat into the hilum

kub-anatomy:struct.q: The renal pelvis forms by the union of:
The left renal vein crosses between the aorta and which artery, where it can be compressed (nutcracker syndrome)?
kub-anatomy:struct.e: The left renal vein passes between the SMA and aorta; it also receives the left gonadal and left adrenal veins.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: Why is the left kidney usually chosen for living-donor transplant?
o: It sits lower than the right
kub-anatomy:struct.e: The left renal vein is longer (crosses the aorta), which makes anastomosis easier.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: Which renal region is most sensitive to hypoxic injury?
o: Outer medulla (PT straight segment and TAL)
kub-anatomy:struct.e: The straight segment of the PT and the thick ascending limb in the outer medulla have high metabolic demand and low O₂ supply, so ischemia hits them first (ATN).

kub-anatomy:struct.q: A surgeon performing a left nephrectomy approaches the renal hilum from the front. Which hilar structure is encountered first?
kub-anatomy:struct.e: At the hilum the order from anterior to posterior is vein, artery, then pelvis (VAP), so the renal vein lies most anterior. The pelvis is the most posterior.

kub-anatomy:vessels.q: Which renal vessel passes posterior to the inferior vena cava?
kub-anatomy:vessels.e: The right renal artery is longer and runs behind the IVC; the long left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta.

kub-anatomy:vessels.q: Which tributary drains into the left renal vein but not the right?
o: Inferior phrenic vein only on the right
kub-anatomy:vessels.e: The left gonadal and left suprarenal veins join the left renal vein; on the right they enter the IVC directly.

kub-anatomy:vessels.q: Why does occlusion of a segmental renal artery cause infarction of that segment?
o: They drain into the vasa recta
They anastomose freely with lumbar arteries
kub-anatomy:vessels.e: There are no effective anastomoses between segments.

kub-anatomy:vessels.q: A 19-year-old man has recurrent episodes of left flank pain after drinking large volumes of beer. CT angiography shows a dilated renal pelvis with a normal-caliber ureter and a vessel crossing anterior to the ureteropelvic junction. The vessel is most likely:
kub-anatomy:vessels.e: Accessory (polar) renal arteries are end arteries that enter the lower pole directly and can compress the UPJ, causing intermittent obstruction with diuresis. The gonadal vein crosses the ureter lower down and does not cause UPJ obstruction.

kub-anatomy:lnn.q: Lymph from the kidneys drains mainly to:
kub-anatomy:lnn.e: Along the renal vessels to para-aortic nodes.

kub-anatomy:lnn.q: Kidney pain is referred to the loin and groin because visceral afferents enter the cord at about:
kub-anatomy:lnn.e: Sympathetic afferents with the renal plexus enter T10–L1.

kub-anatomy:lnn.q: A 63-year-old man has a 7-cm renal cell carcinoma of the left kidney. During staging, which lymph nodes are expected to be involved first?
kub-anatomy:lnn.e: Renal lymphatics follow the renal vessels to the lateral aortic (lumbar) nodes; the left kidney drains to left para-aortic nodes (the right kidney to paracaval/interaortocaval nodes). Internal iliac nodes drain pelvic organs such as the bladder base.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three normal sites of ureteric narrowing?
o: Pelvic brim over the iliac vessels
Where the gonadal vessels cross the ureter
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Stones commonly lodge at the UPJ, pelvic brim and ureterovesical junction.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: In women, the pelvic ureter passes directly beneath the:
o: Ovarian artery in the broad ligament
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: 'Water under the bridge'; at risk during hysterectomy. In men the ductus deferens crosses above it.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Ureteric colic is referred to dermatomes:
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Loin to groin: flank, pubic region, scrotum/labia majora, anterior thigh.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Vesicoureteral reflux is primarily due to:
o: Long oblique submucosal tunnel at the trigone
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: A short intramural segment of the ureter in the bladder wall (short, laterally placed insertion) lacks the flap-valve effect, so urine refluxes; it predisposes to recurrent UTI and pyelonephritis.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: A child with recurrent pyelonephritis is investigated for reflux. The diagnostic test of choice is:
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: VCUG shows contrast refluxing up the ureters during voiding; chronic VUR causes renal scarring (chronic pyelonephritis).

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Reflux is prevented normally because the ureter:
o: Passes obliquely through the bladder wall
Has a sphincter of skeletal muscle
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Bladder pressure compresses the intramural segment.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: The main long-term risk of untreated VUR is:
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Recurrent pyelonephritis scars the kidney → hypertension and CKD.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: In the pelvis, the ureter passes under which structures ("water under the bridge")?
o: Internal iliac vein and obturator nerve
External iliac artery and femoral nerve
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Ureters run retroperitoneally under the gonadal vessels, over the iliacs, and under the uterine artery / vas deferens.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: During hysterectomy, the ureter is most at risk when ligating the:
o: Ovarian artery in the infundibulopelvic ligament only
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: The ureter lies ~2 cm lateral to the cervix, just beneath the uterine artery, so it can be clamped or ligated with it.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: A 35-year-old man has sudden colicky right flank pain radiating to the groin and microscopic hematuria. Non-contrast CT shows a 5-mm stone. At which site is it most likely to lodge?
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: The ureterovesical junction, where the ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall, is the narrowest point and the most common site of stone impaction. The gonadal vessel crossing is not one of the physiologic narrowings.

kub-anatomy:adrenal.q: The left suprarenal vein drains into the:
kub-anatomy:adrenal.e: The right suprarenal vein is very short and enters the IVC directly.

kub-anatomy:adrenal.q: The middle suprarenal artery arises from the:
kub-anatomy:adrenal.e: Superior from the inferior phrenic, middle from the aorta, inferior from the renal artery.

kub-anatomy:adrenal.q: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are innervated by:
o: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers that have not synapsed
Postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the celiac ganglion
kub-anatomy:adrenal.e: The medulla acts like a modified sympathetic ganglion.

kub-anatomy:adrenal.q: A 46-year-old woman with resistant hypertension and K⁺ 2.9 mEq/L has suppressed renin and high aldosterone. She undergoes adrenal vein sampling via the femoral vein. To reach the left adrenal vein, the catheter must pass through which vessel?
kub-anatomy:adrenal.e: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right drains directly into the IVC (short, and harder to cannulate). The left gonadal vein also enters the left renal vein but does not receive adrenal blood.

kub-anatomy:aorta.q: At which vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate?
kub-anatomy:aorta.e: The bifurcation lies about 2.5 cm below the umbilicus, level with the iliac crests.

kub-anatomy:aorta.q: The renal arteries arise from the aorta at about:
kub-anatomy:aorta.e: The left is usually slightly higher; the right is longer.

o: At L4, anterior to the aortic bifurcation
Beside the left renal vein, left of the aorta
At L1–L2, right of and behind the aorta
In the posterior mediastinum at T8
kub-anatomy:aorta.e: It lies anterior to L1–L2, posterior and to the right of the aorta. It receives the intestinal and lumbar trunks and begins the thoracic duct.

kub-anatomy:aorta.q: A 71-year-old male smoker has a pulsatile periumbilical mass. CT shows an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm extending down to the aortic bifurcation. At which vertebral level does the aorta normally bifurcate?
kub-anatomy:aorta.e: The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at about L4, roughly at the level of the umbilicus. The renal arteries arise at about L1–L2.

kub-anatomy:plexus.q: Which branch of the lumbar plexus emerges on the anterior surface of psoas major?
kub-anatomy:plexus.e: Medial border: obturator and lumbosacral trunk; lateral border: iliohypogastric, ilio-inguinal, LFCN, femoral.

kub-anatomy:plexus.q: Which nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas major and passes through the obturator foramen?
kub-anatomy:plexus.e: It supplies the medial thigh muscles and skin.

kub-anatomy:plexus.q: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve arises from:
kub-anatomy:plexus.e: It runs under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS; compression causes meralgia paresthetica.

kub-anatomy:plexus.q: A 68-year-old man on warfarin develops a large retroperitoneal hematoma in the iliopsoas. He has weak knee extension, an absent patellar reflex and numbness of the anterior thigh. Which nerve is compressed?
kub-anatomy:plexus.e: The femoral nerve (L2–L4) emerges from the lateral border of psoas and runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus, where a hematoma compresses it, causing quadriceps weakness and loss of the knee jerk. The obturator nerve supplies the hip adductors.

kub-anatomy:bladder.q: Where is the bladder mucosa smooth and firmly attached to the muscle coat?
kub-anatomy:bladder.e: Elsewhere the mucosa is folded (rugae) and loosely attached.

kub-anatomy:bladder.q: The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the:
kub-anatomy:bladder.e: It runs from the bladder apex to the umbilicus. The medial umbilical ligaments are the obliterated umbilical arteries.

kub-anatomy:bladder.q: Lymph from the base of the bladder drains mainly to the:
kub-anatomy:bladder.e: Superior and inferolateral surfaces → external iliac; neck → sacral nodes.

kub-anatomy:bladder.q: A 24-year-old man with a full bladder after drinking alcohol is kicked in the lower abdomen. Cystography shows contrast outlining loops of bowel and the paracolic gutters. Which part of the bladder is most likely ruptured?
kub-anatomy:bladder.e: A blow to a distended bladder ruptures its weakest, peritoneum-covered dome, causing intraperitoneal extravasation. Anterior or neck injuries (often with pelvic fracture) are extraperitoneal.

kub-anatomy:urethra.q: What is the longest part of the male urethra?
kub-anatomy:urethra.e: Spongy ~15 cm, prostatic 3–4 cm, preprostatic ~1 cm, membranous ~0.5 cm.

kub-anatomy:urethra.q: The ejaculatory ducts open onto the:
o: Bulbar part of the spongy urethra
Navicular fossa of the distal urethra
Seminal colliculus of the prostatic urethra
Membranous urethra within the external sphincter
kub-anatomy:urethra.e: The prostatic utricle opens in the middle of the colliculus with an ejaculatory duct on each side.

kub-anatomy:urethra.q: Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter in the deep perineal pouch?
kub-anatomy:urethra.e: The internal (smooth) sphincter is at the preprostatic part.

kub-anatomy:urethra.q: A 22-year-old man falls astride a beam. He has blood at the urethral meatus and swelling of the scrotum and penis that extends onto the lower anterior abdominal wall but not into the thighs. Which part of the urethra is injured?
kub-anatomy:urethra.e: A straddle injury ruptures the bulbar spongy urethra; urine spreads in the superficial perineal space under Colles fascia, which is continuous with Scarpa fascia but attached to the fascia lata, sparing the thighs. Membranous injuries follow pelvic fractures.

kub-anatomy:clinic.q: The left gonadal vein drains into the:
kub-anatomy:clinic.e: Left renal vein compression (nutcracker) or left RCC may cause left varicocele.

kub-anatomy:clinic.q: During hysterectomy the ureter is at risk where it passes:
kub-anatomy:clinic.e: 'Water under the bridge': the classic site of iatrogenic ureter injury.

kub-anatomy:clinic.q: A 63-year-old man has a new left-sided varicocele that does not decompress when he lies supine. He also reports intermittent hematuria and has a palpable left flank mass. What is the most likely cause of the varicocele?
o: Tumor thrombus in the left renal vein
IVC compression by a hepatic mass
kub-anatomy:clinic.e: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, so renal cell carcinoma extending into that vein obstructs gonadal outflow. An idiopathic varicocele decompresses when supine.

kub-histology:lowpower.q: On a low-power kidney section, a pale striated band runs from the medulla into the cortex but contains no renal corpuscles. What is it?
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Medullary rays are straight tubules (proximal and distal straight parts, collecting tubules) extending into the cortex; corpuscles are absent there.

kub-histology:lowpower.q: Which zone of the renal medulla contains only thin limbs of Henle and collecting ducts?
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Inner medulla = thin limbs (of juxtamedullary nephrons) + large collecting ducts; thick limbs end at the inner–outer medulla border.

o: A medullary ray and surrounding cortex
A minor calyx and its renal papilla
A pyramid and its overlying cortical cap
The territory of one segmental artery
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Lobe = pyramid + overlying cortex. Lobule = a medullary ray + surrounding cortex drained by one collecting duct system.

kub-histology:lowpower.q: The sieve-like tip of a renal papilla where papillary ducts open is called:
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Openings of the papillary ducts (ducts of Bellini) give the papilla tip a perforated appearance: the area cribrosa.

kub-histology:lowpower.q: A needle biopsy is taken from a 42-year-old woman with nephrotic-range proteinuria. The pathologist reports that the core contains only collecting ducts, thin limbs of Henle and vasa recta, with no renal corpuscles. Which region was sampled?
kub-histology:lowpower.e: The inner medulla contains only thin limbs, collecting ducts and vasa recta. Renal corpuscles lie in the cortical labyrinth and the renal columns, so the biopsy is inadequate to assess glomerular disease.

kub-histology:nephron.e: Different embryologic origins: metanephric blastema and ureteric bud.

kub-histology:nephron.q: Which segment has simple squamous epithelium?
kub-histology:nephron.e: Thin limbs are squamous; TAL and DCT are cuboidal.

kub-histology:nephron.q: A 67-year-old man develops AKI after prolonged hypotension during surgery. Biopsy shows necrosis and sloughing of cuboidal cells with brush borders, concentrated in the outer medulla. Which segment is most affected?
kub-histology:nephron.e: Ischemic ATN preferentially injures the straight part of the proximal tubule (brush border) and the thick ascending limb in the hypoxic outer medulla. Thin limbs are simple squamous and lack a brush border.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Blood in the arcuate arteries flows next into:
kub-histology:vessels.e: Interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radial) → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Vasa recta arise from efferent arterioles of:
kub-histology:vessels.e: Juxtamedullary efferents form long straight loops alongside Henle loops; cortical efferents form peritubular capillaries.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Calcium oxalate stones often start as Randall plaques in the basement membrane of:
kub-histology:vessels.e: Randall plaques form in the basement membranes of the thin limbs in the medulla.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Sickle cell disease classically injures the renal papilla because:
o: Vasa recta have low O₂ tension and high osmolality
Glomerular capillaries have the lowest O₂ tension
Collecting ducts lack any capillary blood supply
The papillary urothelium is unusually thin
kub-histology:vessels.e: Hypoxic, hypertonic medulla promotes sickling in the vasa recta → papillary necrosis.

kub-histology:vessels.q: A renal biopsy from a 61-year-old man with long-standing hypertension shows many globally sclerosed glomeruli. The tubules downstream of these glomeruli are atrophic. Which anatomic fact best explains the tubular atrophy?
o: Peritubular capillaries arise from efferent arterioles
Cortical tubules are fed by interlobular arteries
Vasa recta are the only supply of cortical tubules
Tubular cells draw their oxygen from filtrate
kub-histology:vessels.e: Blood reaches the cortical peritubular capillaries only after passing through the glomerulus via the efferent arteriole, so glomerular obliteration starves its downstream tubules. The vasa recta supply the medulla, not cortical tubules.

kub-histology:corpuscle.q: The parietal layer of Bowman capsule is lined by:
kub-histology:corpuscle.e: Parietal layer = simple squamous; it becomes cuboidal at the urinary pole where the PCT begins.

kub-histology:corpuscle.q: Inside a glomerulus on H&E, nuclei that bulge into the urinary space on the outer surface of capillary loops belong to:
kub-histology:corpuscle.e: Podocytes cover the outer (urinary) surface of the loops. Mesangial nuclei sit centrally between loops; endothelial nuclei are flat on the inner side.

kub-histology:corpuscle.q: The urinary pole of a renal corpuscle is where:
o: The macula densa contacts the arterioles
kub-histology:corpuscle.e: Vascular pole = arterioles; urinary (tubular) pole = capsular space opens into the PCT.

kub-histology:corpuscle.q: A 23-year-old man has hemoptysis and hematuria, and his creatinine rises over 3 weeks. Renal biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli with linear IgG along the GBM. The crescents are formed mainly by proliferation of which cells?
o: Parietal epithelial cells of Bowman capsule
kub-histology:corpuscle.e: Crescents in rapidly progressive GN (here Goodpasture) form from proliferating parietal epithelial cells plus infiltrating monocytes/macrophages and fibrin in Bowman space. Mesangial proliferation is typical of IgA nephropathy.

kub-histology:barrier.q: A boy has hematuria, hearing loss and anterior lenticonus with a COL4A5 mutation. Which structure is abnormal on EM?
kub-histology:barrier.e: Alport syndrome: type IV collagen defect → split, laminated GBM.

kub-histology:barrier.q: Which protein forms the zipper-like slit diaphragm between pedicels?
kub-histology:barrier.e: Nephrin molecules from adjacent foot processes interlock; mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome.

kub-histology:barrier.q: The negatively charged layers of the GBM that repel anionic proteins are the:
kub-histology:barrier.e: Both laminae rarae (and the endothelial glycocalyx) carry negative charge; the lamina densa filters mainly by size.

kub-histology:barrier.q: Approximately what fraction of plasma entering a glomerulus is filtered?
A newborn of Finnish descent has massive proteinuria and generalized edema; the placenta was unusually large. The defect most likely involves which component of the filtration barrier?
o: Type IV collagen of the GBM
Heparan sulfate of the laminae rarae
kub-histology:barrier.e: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type is caused by NPHS1 mutations in nephrin, the main protein of the slit diaphragm. Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome, with hematuria rather than massive neonatal proteinuria.

kub-histology:mesangium.q: Which function is NOT performed by intraglomerular mesangial cells?
o: Production of matrix to support capillaries
kub-histology:mesangium.e: Renin comes from juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole, not mesangial cells.

kub-histology:mesangium.q: Extraglomerular mesangial cells are also called:
kub-histology:mesangium.e: Lacis cells fill the space between the afferent and efferent arterioles and the macula densa, forming part of the JGA.

o: Between capillary loops where podocytes are absent
Lining the parietal layer of Bowman capsule as squamous cells
Within the media of the efferent arteriole
kub-histology:mesangium.e: They support capillaries on surfaces not covered by podocytes, sharing a basement membrane with the endothelium.

kub-histology:mesangium.q: A 20-year-old man has painless gross hematuria 2 days after an upper respiratory infection. Biopsy immunofluorescence shows granular deposits of IgA. Where are the deposits mainly located?
kub-histology:mesangium.e: IgA nephropathy is defined by mesangial IgA deposits with mesangial cell proliferation. Subepithelial humps are typical of post-streptococcal GN, which follows infection by 2–3 weeks.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Compared with the PCT, the DCT in cross-section shows:
o: Taller, redder cells with a dense brush border
Columnar cells interspersed with goblet cells
Squamous cells with RBCs in the lumen
Smaller, paler cells and a clear lumen
kub-histology:pctdct.e: DCT: smaller, less eosinophilic cells, no brush border, more nuclei per section, empty lumen.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Why do PCT cells stain so eosinophilic?
o: Abundant rough ER for protein export
kub-histology:pctdct.e: Mitochondria aligned in basal infoldings power Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and give strong acidophilia.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Which stain best highlights the PCT brush border and basement membranes in magenta?
kub-histology:pctdct.e: PAS stains the glycoprotein-rich glycocalyx of microvilli and basement membranes.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Why are PCT sections more numerous than DCT sections in the cortex?
o: The DCT lies in the medulla
The DCT is destroyed during fixation
The PCT has more cells per section
kub-histology:pctdct.e: The PCT is the longest segment, so it is cut more often around corpuscles.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: A renal biopsy from a 55-year-old with ischemic AKI shows many cortical tubules with flattened cells that have lost their PAS-positive apical border. A few intact tubules with smaller, paler cells and wide, clear lumens lie next to the vascular pole, where their wall forms the macula densa. The intact tubules are:
kub-histology:pctdct.e: DCT cells are smaller and paler, lack a brush border and contact the vascular pole at the macula densa. The injured tubules with PAS-positive brush borders are proximal convoluted tubules.

kub-histology:pctem.q: Small proteins filtered at the glomerulus are handled in the PCT by:
o: Secretion back to the capillary as protein
kub-histology:pctem.e: Apical pits and vesicles take up proteins; lysosomes degrade them and amino acids exit basolaterally.

kub-histology:pctem.q: Basal membrane infoldings packed with mitochondria indicate:
kub-histology:pctem.e: This pattern marks cells doing active transport (PCT, TAL, DCT, striated ducts).

kub-histology:pctem.q: Leaky tight junctions in the PCT allow:
o: Transcellular water flow via AQP2 alone
Secretion of glucose back into the lumen
Paracellular movement of water and solutes

kub-histology:pctem.q: The PCT stains intensely eosinophilic in H&E because of:
A 72-year-old woman receives gentamicin for 10 days. Her creatinine rises, and urinalysis shows muddy brown granular casts. The drug accumulates in proximal tubule cells mainly by which mechanism?
kub-histology:pctem.e: Filtered aminoglycosides bind megalin on the PCT brush border and are taken up by endocytosis, accumulating in lysosomes and causing ATN. Paracellular movement does not concentrate drug inside cells.

kub-histology:medulla.q: In the medulla, how is a thin limb of Henle told apart from a vasa recta capillary?
o: Thinner epithelium and RBCs in the lumen
A short apical brush border on its cells
Pericytes surrounding the thin limb wall
Thicker epithelium and no RBCs in the lumen
kub-histology:medulla.e: Thin limb epithelium is slightly thicker and its lumen lacks RBCs. Both are squamous, but capillaries are thinner and usually contain erythrocytes.

kub-histology:medulla.q: Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin), the matrix of urinary casts, is made by:
kub-histology:medulla.e: Only the TAL epithelium produces Tamm-Horsfall protein.

kub-histology:medulla.q: Which segment is permeable to water but relatively impermeable to NaCl?
kub-histology:medulla.e: Thin descending limb lets water leave into the hyperosmotic interstitium; the ascending limbs are water-tight.

kub-histology:medulla.q: A 66-year-old man with bone pain, anemia and hypercalcemia develops AKI. Biopsy shows large, fractured, eosinophilic casts in distal tubules surrounded by giant cells. The casts form when light chains bind a protein secreted by which segment?
kub-histology:medulla.e: Myeloma cast nephropathy results from light chains binding Tamm–Horsfall protein (uromodulin), which is secreted by the thick ascending limb. The PCT reabsorbs light chains but does not make the cast matrix.

kub-histology:jga.q: Renin-containing granular cells of the JGA are modified:
o: Smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
Endothelial cells of the efferent arteriole
kub-histology:jga.e: JG cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the tunica media of the afferent arteriole.

kub-histology:jga.q: Macula densa cells are distinguished on a slide by:
o: Tall, crowded cells with apically placed nuclei
Cuboidal cells with a prominent brush border
Binucleate dome-shaped cells bulging into the lumen
Many flattened nuclei along a thin wall
kub-histology:jga.e: Macula densa: closely packed columnar cells of the distal tubule with apical nuclei and basal Golgi.
Macula densa = chemoreceptor for luminal NaCl (tubuloglomerular feedback); JG cells act as baroreceptors.

kub-histology:jga.q: A 15-year-old boy has severe hypertension (190/115 mmHg), K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L, very high plasma renin activity and normal renal arteries on angiography. CT shows a 2-cm well-circumscribed renal cortical tumor. The tumor most likely arises from which cells?
o: Principal cells of the collecting duct
kub-histology:jga.e: A juxtaglomerular cell tumor (reninoma) arises from the renin-secreting granular cells, which are modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole. Macula densa cells sense NaCl but do not secrete renin.

kub-histology:cd.q: An antibody to aquaporin-2 would stain which cells most intensely after ADH?
kub-histology:cd.e: ADH inserts AQP2-containing vesicles into the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells.

kub-histology:cd.q: Collecting duct cells are recognized on H&E by:
o: Pale cytoplasm and distinct cell borders
Strong eosinophilia and a brush border
kub-histology:cd.e: Principal cells have few organelles (pale) and sharp lateral borders, unlike the interdigitating tubule cells.
α-intercalated cells secrete H⁺; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO₃⁻. Both are darker and mitochondria-rich.

kub-histology:cd.q: A 47-year-old woman on long-term lithium has a urine output of 6 L/day. Urine osmolality stays at 120 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. Lithium enters and damages which cells through ENaC?
kub-histology:cd.e: Lithium enters collecting duct principal cells via ENaC and reduces aquaporin-2 expression, causing nephrogenic DI; amiloride limits this entry. Intercalated cells handle acid–base, not ADH-regulated water transport.

kub-histology:slideid.q: A medullary tubule with pale cells and sharp cell borders is most likely a:
kub-histology:slideid.e: Principal cells have few organelles and distinct lateral borders.

kub-histology:slideid.q: A thin-walled medullary profile containing red blood cells is a:
kub-histology:slideid.e: Thin limbs look similar but lack RBCs.

kub-histology:slideid.q: A resected renal papilla from a 58-year-old with chronic analgesic use shows papillary necrosis. At the tip, intact areas show large ducts lined by tall columnar cells with pale cytoplasm opening onto the surface. These ducts are:
kub-histology:slideid.e: Papillary ducts are the terminal collecting ducts, lined by tall pale columnar cells, opening at the area cribrosa. Thin limbs are lined by simple squamous cells and are small.

kub-histology:urothelium.q: Plaques of uroplakin in the apical membrane of umbrella cells serve to:
o: Move urine by coordinated ciliary beating
Absorb water from urine via aquaporins
Seal the barrier while allowing distension
Secrete mucus that protects the surface
kub-histology:urothelium.e: They form an osmotic barrier: rigid uroplakin plaques joined by hinges fold into vesicles when empty and unfold when full, keeping the barrier intact.

kub-histology:urothelium.q: When the bladder fills, the urothelium:
o: Thickens as umbrella cells become cuboidal
Loses its basement membrane as it stretches
Thins to 2–3 layers with flat umbrella cells
kub-histology:urothelium.e: It thins from about 5–7 to 2–3 cell layers; cells shift laterally and flatten, and full urothelium can mimic stratified squamous.

kub-histology:urothelium.q: Which part of the urinary system has epithelial membranes with stiffened protein plaques?
kub-histology:urothelium.e: Umbrella cells of the bladder urothelium carry uroplakin plaques.

kub-histology:urothelium.q: Cystoscopy for microscopic hematuria in a 64-year-old man is normal. A biopsy taken while the bladder was distended shows urothelium only 2–3 cells thick, with flattened surface cells. What is the best interpretation?
kub-histology:urothelium.e: Urothelium thins to 2–3 layers with flattened umbrella cells when the bladder is distended; this is normal. Squamous metaplasia would show stratified squamous cells, often keratinized.

kub-histology:ureter.q: The muscularis of the upper two-thirds of the ureter is arranged as:
kub-histology:ureter.e: Upper ureter: inner longitudinal + outer circular; an outer longitudinal layer is added in the lower third.

kub-histology:ureter.q: Which epithelium lines the prostatic urethra?
kub-histology:ureter.e: Prostatic urethra = urothelium; membranous and spongy = stratified/pseudostratified columnar; distal end = stratified squamous.

kub-histology:ureter.q: The superior surface (dome) of the bladder is covered by:
kub-histology:ureter.e: Only the dome is covered by peritoneum (serosa); elsewhere adventitia.

kub-histology:ureter.q: A ureter in cross-section has a star-shaped lumen because:
o: Its mucosa folds when the lumen is empty
Its striated muscle contracts in spirals
kub-histology:ureter.e: Longitudinal mucosal folds form when the undistended ureter contracts.

kub-histology:ureter.q: A pathologist examines a ureter removed in a nephroureterectomy specimen. One cross-section shows a muscularis with inner longitudinal, middle circular and outer longitudinal layers. This section most likely comes from the:
kub-histology:ureter.e: The ureter has two muscle layers (inner longitudinal, outer circular) in its upper two-thirds and gains an outer longitudinal layer in its lower third. The renal pelvis and UPJ have the two-layer pattern.

kub-histology:bladder.q: The detrusor muscle is arranged as:
o: Inner circular, middle longitudinal, outer circular
Inner circular and outer longitudinal layers
Striated skeletal muscle in three layers
Inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal
kub-histology:bladder.e: Layers intermingle except near the bladder neck.

kub-histology:bladder.q: Only the superior surface of the bladder has a:

A transurethral resection specimen from a 69-year-old smoker shows high-grade urothelial carcinoma. To decide whether the tumor is muscle-invasive (stage T2), which layer must be present in the specimen?
kub-histology:bladder.e: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer means invasion of the detrusor (muscularis propria), so it must be sampled for staging. Invasion of the thin, discontinuous muscularis mucosae is still non-muscle-invasive (T1).

kub-histology:urethra.q: The female urethra is lined proximally by urothelium and distally by:
The membranous urethra in males passes through the:
o: Internal sphincter at the bladder neck

kub-histology:urethra.q: A 26-year-old man has purulent urethral discharge from gonococcal urethritis. The organism adheres to the epithelium lining most of the spongy urethra. Which epithelium is this?
kub-histology:urethra.e: Most of the spongy urethra is lined by pseudostratified (to stratified) columnar epithelium, becoming stratified squamous at the navicular fossa. Urothelium lines the prostatic urethra.

kub-histology:clinical.q: In acute pyelonephritis neutrophils accumulate especially in the:
kub-histology:clinical.e: Ascending infection reaches the papilla first.

kub-histology:clinical.q: A 4-year-old boy has periorbital and leg edema, with a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 6 mg/mg and a normal creatinine. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy is unremarkable. Which electron microscopy finding is expected?
kub-histology:clinical.e: Minimal change disease shows normal light microscopy with diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on EM. Subepithelial humps are seen in post-streptococcal GN.

renal-ch25:balance.q: Normal daily insensible water loss is about:
Water formed by metabolism adds about:
renal-ch25:balance.e: From oxidation of carbohydrates; total intake ~2300 mL/day.

renal-ch25:balance.q: During prolonged heavy exercise in heat, the largest water loss is through:

A 30-year-old man with 40% second- and third-degree burns needs much more IV fluid than expected, even though he has no fever and normal urine output. What is the main mechanism of his increased water loss?
o: Loss of the cornified skin layer
renal-ch25:balance.e: The cornified layer normally limits insensible evaporation from the skin; when burns destroy it, evaporative loss can rise to several liters per day. Sweat glands are destroyed, not stimulated, in deep burns.

renal-ch25:compartments.q: Using the 60-40-20 rule, what fraction of body weight is extracellular fluid?
renal-ch25:compartments.e: Total body water ≈ 60% of weight; ICF 40%, ECF 20% (interstitial ¾, plasma ¼).

renal-ch25:compartments.q: Which substance is used to measure extracellular fluid volume?
renal-ch25:compartments.e: Inulin stays in the ECF. Albumin/Evans blue mark plasma; tritiated water marks total body water.

renal-ch25:compartments.q: In a 70-kg man, interstitial fluid volume is about:
renal-ch25:compartments.e: ECF 14 L = interstitial ~11 L + plasma ~3 L.

renal-ch25:compartments.q: Intracellular fluid volume is calculated as:

An 82-year-old woman becomes dehydrated more quickly than her 25-year-old grandson during a heat wave. Compared with him, her total body water as a percentage of body weight is lower mainly because of her:
renal-ch25:compartments.e: Fat contains little water, so women and older people (more fat, less muscle) have a lower TBW percentage (about 50% or less vs. 60%). Bone density in the elderly is usually lower, not higher.

renal-ch25:composition.q: Plasma has slightly higher cation concentration than interstitial fluid because of:
o: Active Na⁺ pumping by capillary endothelium
Continuous lymph flow out of the interstitium
renal-ch25:composition.e: Negatively charged plasma proteins retain cations in plasma (Gibbs–Donnan effect).

renal-ch25:composition.q: A 35-year-old man is pulled from earthquake rubble after his legs were trapped for 8 hours. Soon after the release, he develops peaked T waves and a wide QRS complex. Release of which ion from damaged cells explains these findings?
renal-ch25:composition.e: K⁺ is the major intracellular cation, and crush injury (rhabdomyolysis) releases it into the ECF, causing hyperkalemia. Na⁺ is mainly extracellular, and Ca²⁺ actually falls as it deposits in injured muscle.

renal-ch25:measure.e: These bind albumin and stay in plasma.

renal-ch25:measure.q: Interstitial fluid volume is calculated as:
If 100 mg of a substance distributes evenly to 7.1 mg/L, its volume of distribution is about:
In a 70-kg volunteer, 10 mg of Evans blue is injected IV. After mixing, the plasma concentration is 3.33 mg/L; the hematocrit is 45%. What is the total blood volume?
renal-ch25:measure.e: Plasma volume = 10 mg ÷ 3.33 mg/L = 3.0 L, and blood volume = plasma volume ÷ (1 − Hct) = 3.0 ÷ 0.55 ≈ 5.5 L. Answering 3.0 L stops at plasma volume.

renal-ch25:osmosis.q: Each mOsm/L concentration gradient produces about how much osmotic pressure?
renal-ch25:osmosis.e: At 282 mOsm/L the potential pressure exceeds 5400 mmHg.

renal-ch25:osmosis.q: A cell placed in a hypotonic solution will:
A 66-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes has plasma glucose 900 mg/dL, Na⁺ 132 mEq/L and confusion. What happens to the volume of his brain cells?
o: Swell, because plasma Na⁺ is low
Shrink, as glucose is an effective osmole
No change, as glucose is an ineffective osmole
Swell, because glucose enters the cells
renal-ch25:osmosis.e: Without insulin, glucose stays extracellular and acts as an effective osmole, drawing water out of cells (high effective osmolality despite low measured Na⁺). Urea, not glucose, is the classic ineffective osmole.

renal-ch25:shifts.q: Two liters of 3% NaCl are infused into a 70-kg man. After osmotic equilibrium, which is true?
o: ICF volume increases and ECF volume decreases
ECF volume increases and ICF volume decreases
Both ECF and ICF volumes increase equally
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Hypertonic saline raises ECF osmolarity, pulling water out of cells: ECF ↑, ICF ↓ (Guyton: ECF 19 L, ICF 25 L, 313.9 mOsm/L).
Isotonic fluid stays in the ECF; no osmotic gradient forms across cell membranes.

renal-ch25:shifts.q: Why does 5% dextrose behave like free water after infusion?
o: It stays in the plasma compartment
It is excreted unchanged in urine
It is markedly hypertonic to plasma
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Glucose enters cells and is metabolized, so the net effect is adding solute-free water.

renal-ch25:shifts.q: Plasma osmolarity can be estimated at the bedside mainly from:
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Na⁺ and its anions account for most ECF osmoles: osmolarity ≈ 2 × [Na⁺].

renal-ch25:shifts.q: A solute that crosses cell membranes freely (urea) at the same osmolarity as plasma is:
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Tonicity depends on impermeant solutes; urea equilibrates across membranes, so cells eventually swell.

renal-ch25:shifts.q: A 28-year-old hiker is lost in the desert without water for 2 days, losing mainly pure water. Compared with normal, which change in body fluids is expected?
o: ↓ ECF, no ICF change, same osmolarity
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Water loss raises ECF osmolarity, which draws water out of cells, so both compartments shrink and osmolarity rises. Isotonic losses (such as diarrhea) shrink only the ECF.

renal-ch25:natremia.e: Excess ADH retains water → ECF and ICF expand with low Na⁺ (Table 25-4).

renal-ch25:natremia.q: Chronic hyponatremia should be corrected slowly to avoid:
renal-ch25:natremia.e: Guyton: limit correction to <10–12 mmol/L in 24 h and <18 mmol/L in 48 h.

renal-ch25:natremia.q: The total safety factor against edema is about:
renal-ch25:natremia.e: Low compliance 3 + lymph flow 7 + protein washdown 7 ≈ 17 mmHg.

renal-ch25:natremia.q: Edema in nephrotic syndrome is mainly due to:
renal-ch25:natremia.e: Loss of albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, increasing net filtration into tissues.

renal-ch25:natremia.q: A 32-year-old woman collapses after a marathon during which she drank water at every station. She is confused. Na⁺ is 121 mEq/L and plasma osmolality 252 mOsm/kg. Her confusion is best explained by:
o: Water moving out of brain cells
renal-ch25:natremia.e: Excess water intake lowers plasma osmolality, so water moves into brain cells and causes cerebral edema. Pontine demyelination results from overly rapid correction, not from the hyponatremia itself.

renal-ch25:edema.q: Which is NOT a cause of increased capillary filtration?
renal-ch25:edema.e: Low (not high) plasma proteins cause edema.

renal-ch25:edema.q: Lymphatic obstruction from filariasis causes edema because:
renal-ch25:edema.e: Lymph cannot return protein and fluid.

renal-ch25:edema.q: Fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity is called:
A 52-year-old woman develops gradually increasing, firm, non-pitting swelling of her right arm 1 year after mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. What is the main mechanism?
renal-ch25:edema.e: Removing axillary nodes blocks lymph drainage, so filtered protein accumulates in the interstitium and holds fluid (lymphedema). Low plasma oncotic pressure would cause generalized, pitting edema.

renal-ch26:overview.q: Which kidney cell type makes erythropoietin in response to hypoxia?
renal-ch26:overview.e: EPO comes from peritubular interstitial cells. CKD → normocytic anemia.

renal-ch26:overview.q: 1α-hydroxylase, which makes calcitriol, is located in the:
renal-ch26:overview.e: PTH stimulates and FGF23 inhibits PCT 1α-hydroxylase; CKD → ↓ calcitriol.

renal-ch26:overview.q: During prolonged fasting, the kidney contributes to plasma glucose via:
renal-ch26:overview.e: Guyton lists renal gluconeogenesis as a kidney function.

renal-ch26:overview.q: A 58-year-old man with stage 4 CKD has fatigue and Hb 8.9 g/dL with normocytic red cells, a low reticulocyte count and normal iron studies. The deficient hormone is normally produced by which cells?
renal-ch26:overview.e: Erythropoietin is made by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the cortex and outer medulla in response to hypoxia. JG cells secrete renin, and PCT cells make calcitriol.

renal-ch26:micturition.q: The micturition reflex is mediated by sensory and motor fibers in the:
renal-ch26:micturition.e: Parasympathetic pelvic nerves (S2–S3); pudendal supplies the external sphincter.

renal-ch26:micturition.q: On a cystometrogram, pressure rises sharply after bladder volume exceeds about:

o: Spinal cord lesion above sacral levels
Destruction of sensory fibers from the bladder
renal-ch26:micturition.e: e.g., crush injury of sacral roots, tabes dorsalis → overflow incontinence.

renal-ch26:micturition.q: A 61-year-old man with long-standing diabetes has a large, painless bladder and dribbling incontinence. On cystometry, the bladder fills to 900 mL with little rise in pressure and no sensation of fullness. Which lesion best explains these findings?
o: Lesion of the pontine micturition center
renal-ch26:micturition.e: Diabetic neuropathy destroys sensory (afferent) fibers from the bladder, abolishing the stretch-triggered micturition reflex and producing an atonic, overfilled bladder. A lesion above the sacral cord instead produces a reflex (spastic) bladder.

renal-ch26:urineform.e: The four processes of urine formation.

renal-ch26:urineform.q: A substance filtered and also secreted, like PAH, is excreted at a rate:
If tubular reabsorption fell by 10% with GFR unchanged, urine volume would rise from 1.5 L/day to about:

A 40-year-old man with neurosyphilis is treated with daily IM procaine penicillin G plus oral probenecid, which keeps serum penicillin levels higher for longer. Probenecid achieves this by inhibiting which renal process?
renal-ch26:urineform.e: Penicillin is excreted largely by organic anion transporter (OAT) secretion in the PCT; probenecid competes for this transporter, reducing excretion. Glomerular filtration is unaffected, and reabsorption would raise, not lower, penicillin levels.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Loss of which component of the glomerular filtration barrier best explains selective albuminuria?
o: Negative charge of the basement membrane
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Heparan sulfate gives the GBM its negative charge, which repels albumin. Loss of charge (e.g., minimal change disease) lets albumin through.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Podocyte foot processes are linked by slit diaphragms containing which protein?
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Nephrin (NPHS1) mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Which layer of the barrier filters mainly by size?
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Laminae rarae and glycocalyx provide charge selectivity.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Albumin is restricted from filtration mainly because of its:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Albumin (6 nm) is smaller than pores (~8 nm) but repelled by negative charges.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Which substance gives the most accurate measurement of GFR?
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Creatinine slightly overestimates GFR because a little is secreted.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Creatinine clearance overestimates GFR because creatinine is:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: A small amount is secreted, so clearance > true GFR by roughly 10–20%.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: If GFR falls to 50% of normal, steady-state plasma creatinine will:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Creatinine excretion = GFR × Pcr; with constant production Pcr doubles.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Constriction of the efferent arteriole (e.g., by angiotensin II) has what effect?
o: ↑ RPF, ↑ GFR, no change in FF
↓ RPF, ↓ GFR, no change in FF
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure (↑ GFR) while reducing plasma flow, so FF = GFR/RPF rises.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: A patient takes high-dose NSAIDs. What happens at the afferent arteriole?
o: No change in tone or GFR
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole; NSAIDs remove this, so it constricts (↓ RPF, ↓ GFR) and can precipitate AKI, especially with ACE inhibitors and diuretics.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Ureteral obstruction changes GFR mainly by:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Back-pressure raises P(BS), opposing filtration and lowering GFR.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: A 74-year-old woman taking lisinopril and furosemide for heart failure starts high-dose ibuprofen for knee pain. One week later her creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.3 mg/dL. Which combination of arteriolar changes best explains the fall in GFR?
renal-ch26:gfr.e: NSAIDs remove prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole, and ACE inhibitors remove angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole; both lower glomerular pressure. Diuretic-induced volume depletion makes the kidney depend on both mechanisms.

renal-ch26:rbf.q: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts which vessel?
renal-ch26:rbf.e: Efferent constriction helps maintain GFR when arterial pressure or volume is low.

renal-ch26:rbf.q: NSAIDs can precipitate acute kidney injury in volume-depleted patients because they block:
o: Angiotensin II that constricts the efferent arteriole
ADH that inserts aquaporins in collecting ducts
Prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole
renal-ch26:rbf.e: Prostaglandins buffer vasoconstriction; blocking them lowers RBF and GFR.

renal-ch26:rbf.q: The kidneys receive about what fraction of cardiac output?
renal-ch26:rbf.e: RBF ≈ 1100 mL/min, about 22% of cardiac output.
Intense sympathetic stimulation constricts renal arterioles, lowering RBF and GFR.

renal-ch26:rbf.q: A 23-year-old woman has 3 days of severe vomiting and is volume depleted. Her renal plasma flow falls more than her GFR, so her filtration fraction rises. What best explains the increased filtration fraction?
renal-ch26:rbf.e: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, lowering RPF while maintaining glomerular pressure and GFR, so GFR/RPF rises. Afferent dilation would raise both RPF and GFR.

renal-ch26:autoreg.q: GFR and RBF are autoregulated over a mean arterial pressure range of about:
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: Autoregulation keeps GFR and RBF relatively constant between ~75 and 160 mmHg.

renal-ch26:autoreg.q: Decreased NaCl at the macula densa causes:
o: Afferent dilation and increased renin release
Afferent constriction and decreased glomerular filtration
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: Tubuloglomerular feedback dilates the afferent arteriole and stimulates renin → Ang II constricts the efferent.

o: Luminal NaCl at the macula densa
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: Stretch opens Ca²⁺ channels in vascular smooth muscle → contraction, limiting transmitted pressure.

renal-ch26:autoreg.q: A high-protein meal increases GFR because:
o: Kf falls as mesangial cells contract
Plasma oncotic pressure rises after absorption
Amino acid–Na⁺ cotransport lowers macula densa NaCl
Amino acids directly dilate the efferent arteriole
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: More Na⁺ is reabsorbed with amino acids in the PCT, so less NaCl reaches the macula densa; TGF-mediated afferent dilation raises GFR.

renal-ch26:autoreg.q: A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria starts empagliflozin. His eGFR falls by about 4 mL/min/1.73 m² in the first weeks and then stabilizes, with slower progression over time. What is the mechanism of the initial fall?
o: Direct podocyte injury by the drug
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: SGLT2 inhibition raises NaCl delivery to the macula densa, which restores tubuloglomerular feedback, constricts the afferent arteriole and reduces hyperfiltration. Efferent dilation is the mechanism of ACE inhibitors and ARBs.

renal-ch27:transport.q: At what plasma glucose concentration does glucose first appear in urine (threshold)?
renal-ch27:transport.e: Glucosuria begins ~200 mg/dL; SGLT transporters are fully saturated (Tm) ~375 mg/dL.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule mainly by:
renal-ch27:transport.e: SGLT2 in the early PCT reabsorbs most glucose; SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozins) cause glucosuria.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Pregnancy commonly causes glucosuria at normal plasma glucose because:
o: ↑ GFR raises filtered load and ↓ proximal reabsorption
Placental hormones block SGLT1 in the gut
Insulin resistance raises plasma glucose above 375
renal-ch27:transport.e: Higher GFR and reduced proximal reabsorption during pregnancy lower the effective threshold.

renal-ch27:transport.q: The transport maximum for glucose is about:
renal-ch27:transport.e: Tm ≈ 375 mg/min; filtered load at normal plasma glucose ≈ 125 mg/min.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Glucose appears in urine before Tm is reached because of:
renal-ch27:transport.e: Splay: nephrons differ in Tm and filtered load, so threshold (~200 mg/min) is below Tm because not all nephrons saturate together.

renal-ch27:transport.q: SGLT2 in the PCT is an example of:
renal-ch27:transport.e: Glucose rides the Na⁺ gradient created by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Proteins filtered at the glomerulus are reabsorbed in the PCT by:
renal-ch27:transport.e: Pinocytosis at the brush border, then lysosomal digestion.

renal-ch27:transport.q: A healthy 21-year-old has 2+ glucose on a routine urine dipstick. Fasting glucose is 84 mg/dL and HbA1c 5.0%; there is no aminoaciduria, phosphaturia or acidosis. A mutation in which transporter is most likely?
renal-ch27:transport.e: Isolated familial renal glucosuria results from SLC5A2 (SGLT2) mutations that lower the glucose Tm, so glucose appears in urine at normal plasma levels. Generalized PCT dysfunction would suggest Fanconi syndrome.

renal-ch27:pct.q: The PCT reabsorbs about what fraction of filtered Na⁺ and water?
Along the PCT, the TF/P ratio of inulin rises because:
o: Water is reabsorbed, inulin is not
Plasma inulin falls along the tubule
Inulin is secreted by PCT cells
renal-ch27:pct.e: Water is reabsorbed while inulin remains, so TF/P inulin indexes water reabsorption.

renal-ch27:pct.q: Organic anions such as penicillin and PAH are secreted in the:
renal-ch27:pct.e: Organic anion transporters on the basolateral membrane.

renal-ch27:pct.q: A 48-year-old man starts cimetidine. Two weeks later his serum creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 1.3 mg/dL, with unchanged urine output, a normal urinalysis and an unchanged cystatin C. What is the most likely mechanism?
renal-ch27:pct.e: Cimetidine (like trimethoprim) blocks proximal tubular secretion of creatinine, raising serum creatinine without changing true GFR (cystatin C unchanged). Interstitial nephritis would produce an abnormal urinalysis.

renal-ch27:loop.q: Which segment reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na⁺ but is impermeable to water?
